item.title: Why Did Atari Fail? The Company That Buried Its Games in the Desert
item.itunes:title: Why Did Atari Fail? The Company That Buried Its Games in the Desert
item.description:
Why did Atari fail? In September 1983, trucks dumped Atari game cartridges in a New Mexico landfill and workers poured concrete over them. One year earlier, Atari was bringing in about $2 billion a year.

This is the story of Atari: the $500 start, Pong, the quarters that jammed the first machine, the Atari 2600, the programmers who walked out and founded Activision, twelve million Pac-Man cartridges, the E.T. game built in about five weeks, the crash of 1983, and the Alamogordo dig in 2014.

Watch this Empire File with photos and documents on YouTube: https://youtu.be/_VbSVRiAzDk
Subscribe on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@riseundruin

Sources
- Encyclopedia.com, Atari Corporation company history (founding, Warner purchase, revenue, 1983 losses, 1984 split): https://www.encyclopedia.com/books/politics-and-business-magazines/atari-corporation
- CNBC, Ted Dabney, a founder of Atari and a creator of Pong: https://www.cnbc.com/2018/06/01/ted-dabney-a-founder-of-atari-and-a-creator-of-pong-dies-at-81.html
- IEEE Spectrum, the Atari 2600 (Consumer Electronics Hall of Fame): https://spectrum.ieee.org/the-consumer-electronics-hall-of-fame-atari-2600
- Game Informer, how four programmers founded Activision: https://gameinformer.com/b/features/archive/2013/02/26/activisionaries-how-four-programmers-changed-the-game-industry-forever
- Time, E.T. for the Atari 2600: https://entertainment.time.com/2012/05/25/et-at-30/slide/the-worst-video-game-of-all-time/
- KMUW, the video game crash: https://www.kmuw.org/your-move/2017-05-18/video-game-crash-your-move
- CBS News (AP), diggers find Atari's E.T. games in the landfill (April 2014; about 728,000 cartridges buried, per former Atari manager James Heller): https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/diggers-find-ataris-et-games-in-landfill

Narrated with an AI voice. Researched and fact-checked by the Rise & Ruin team.

item.title: Why Did Pan Am Fail? The Airline That Took Reservations for the Moon
item.itunes:title: Why Did Pan Am Fail? The Airline That Took Reservations for the Moon
item.description:
Why did Pan Am fail? More than 93,000 people signed up for Pan Am's first flights to the Moon. Twenty years later, the airline that defined the jet age was gone.

This is the story of Pan Am: the Key West mail route, the Clipper flying boats, the first American jet across the Atlantic, the Boeing 747 bet, the First Moon Flights Club, the National Airlines merger, the sale of its crown jewels, and the end in December 1991.

Watch this Empire File with photos and documents on YouTube: https://youtu.be/-kn_wGY0kfU
Subscribe on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@riseundruin

Sources
- Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, the First Moon Flights Club (over 93,000 cards, 1968 to 1971): https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/were-you-member-%E2%80%9Cfirst-moon-flights%E2%80%9D-club
- Smithsonian Air & Space, the 707 flight that changed everything (Oct 26, 1958, New York to Paris): https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/707-flight-changed-everything-180971219/
- U.S. Centennial of Flight Commission, Pan Am history (Oct 19, 1927 first flight, Clippers, 747): https://centennialofflight.net/essay/Commercial_Aviation/Pan_Am/Tran12.htm
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pan American World Airways (1936 Pacific, 1939 Atlantic, 1947 round the world, 1991 bankruptcy and shutdown): https://www.britannica.com/print/article/440588
- The Pan Am Museum, the Boeing 747 (25 ordered in 1966, first passenger flight Jan 22, 1970): https://thepanammuseum.org/exhibit/when-things-get-jumbo
- Pan Am Historical Foundation, the Pan Am Building (1963, sold to MetLife for $400 million): https://www.panam.org/jet-age/air-rights-the-pan-am-building-2

- Airways Magazine, United buys Pan Am's Pacific Division ($750 million): https://airwaysmag.com/united-pan-am-pacific-division

- Delta Flight Museum, Pan Am (routes and shuttle acquired in 1991): https://www.deltamuseum.org/delta-history/family-tree/pan-am
- Deseret News, Dec 5, 1991, Pan Am grounded permanently (about 7,500 jobs): https://www.deseret.com/1991/12/5/18955296/pan-am-grounded-permanently/

item.title: Enron Was America's Most Innovative Company. Its Profits Were Invented
item.itunes:title: Enron Was America's Most Innovative Company. Its Profits Were Invented
item.description:
In August 2000, Enron's stock hit $90. Fifteen months later it was worth 61 cents. Fortune had called it the most innovative large company in America. What it was really inventing was its profits.

This is the story of how a gas pipeline company became a Wall Street star: mark to market accounting, the Blockbuster streaming deal, the hidden side companies, the warning letter, and the biggest bankruptcy in American history at the time.

Watch this Empire File with photos and documents on YouTube: https://youtu.be/o1LHMGajD-s
Subscribe on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@riseundruin

Sources
- Famous Trials (UMKC), Enron chronology (1985 merger, 1992 mark to market approval, $90 stock high, Skilling resignation, Watkins letter, Dynegy, $0.61, bankruptcy, Andersen, convictions): https://famous-trials.com/enron/1789-chronology
- International Banker, The Enron scandal (2001) ($68B peak value, Blockbuster deal profit, Fastow $45M, Andersen $52M fees, $63.4B assets, 4,000 jobs, sentences): https://internationalbanker.com/history-of-financial-crises/the-enron-scandal-2001/
- ABA Journal, Dec. 2, 2001: Enron files for bankruptcy: https://abajournal.com/magazine/article/dec_2_2001_enron_files_for_bankruptcy
- Congressional Research Service, Enron bankruptcy and employer stock in retirement plans (62% of 401(k) assets in Enron stock): https://legistorm.com/reports/view/crs/216324/Enron_Bankruptcy_and_Employer_Stock_in_Retirement_Plans.html
- IDM, Enron in broadband scam (Blockbuster deal ended March 2001): https://idm.net.au/node/5246

item.title: Lehman Brothers Survived 158 Years. It Didn't Survive One Weekend
item.itunes:title: Lehman Brothers Survived 158 Years. It Didn't Survive One Weekend
item.description:
On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy with $639 billion in assets, the biggest bankruptcy in American history. The firm had lived through the Civil War and the Great Depression. It didn't survive one weekend in 2008.

This is the story of a small Alabama store that became a giant of Wall Street: the cotton trade, the housing bet, borrowing at 30 to 1, the Repo 105 accounting trick, and the weekend nobody came to the rescue.

Watch this Empire File with photos and documents on YouTube: https://youtu.be/AaAzwIjWbww
Subscribe on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@riseundruin

Sources
- History.com, Lehman Brothers collapses (1844 founding, $639B assets, $613B debts, 25,000 employees, five mortgage lenders, $111B real estate assets, Dow fell 500+ points, Barclays): https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/september-15/lehman-brothers-collapses
- Harvard Business School Baker Library, Lehman Brothers: general merchants to commodities brokers (Henry, Emanuel and Mayer Lehman, cotton, New York Cotton Exchange): https://www.library.hbs.edu/special-collections-and-archives/exhibits/lehman/general-merchants-to-commodities-brokers
- The Saturday Evening Post (2019), Lehman Brothers: the company that nearly bankrupted America ($360M sale in 1984, 1994 spin-off, roughly 30 to 1 leverage, 45% share drop): https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/2019/01/lehman-brothers-the-company-that-nearly-bankrupted-america/

- Mail & Guardian (2010), Lehman's illegal gimmicks (Repo 105, up to $50B, examiner's report): https://mg.co.za/business/2010-03-23-lehman-s-illegal-gimmicks/

item.title: Sears Quit Selling From Home One Year Before Amazon
item.itunes:title: Sears Quit Selling From Home One Year Before Amazon
item.description:
In 1993, Sears shut down its famous catalog. One year later, Amazon was founded. Sears had been selling to people at home for a hundred years.

This is the story of the store that sold everything: the watch seller from Minnesota, the catalog that sold entire houses, the tallest building in the world, the Kmart deal, and the slow sale of everything Sears owned.

Watch this Empire File with photos and documents on YouTube: https://youtu.be/e8OdW9-D-MI
Subscribe on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@riseundruin

Sources
- History.com, Sears catalog sold everything from houses to hubcaps (1886 watches, Alvah Roebuck, 322 pages in 1894, 70,000 to 75,000 kit homes from 1908 to 1940): https://www.history.com/articles/sears-catalog-houses-hubcaps
- Fox Business (Oct 2018), Sears through the years (1893 name, Kenmore 1913, Craftsman 1927 for $500 and 2017 sale for $900M, Allstate 1931, Sears Tower 1973, Discover 1985, catalog ended 1993): https://www.foxbusiness.com/markets/sears-through-the-years-from-watch-seller-to-tower-builder
- The Motley Fool (Oct 2018), Now-bankrupt Sears was once the Amazon and Walmart (Walmart passed Sears by 1991): https://www.fool.com/investing/2018/10/16/now-bankrupt-sears-was-once-the-amazon-and-walmart.aspx
- PCWorld, Exploring the lost world of Prodigy (run by IBM and Sears, 1988 to 1996): https://www.pcworld.com/article/419660/this-old-tech-exploring-the-lost-world-of-prodigy-one-screen-at-a-time.html
- NBC News (Nov 2004), Kmart to acquire Sears in $11 billion deal (about 3,500 stores, third biggest US retailer): https://www.nbcnews.com/id/6509683/
- The Motley Fool (Oct 2018), Sears bankruptcy: how it got here ($11.3B liabilities, Lands' End, Seritage, store closures): https://www.fool.com/investing/2018/10/15/sears-bankruptcy-how-it-got-here-and-what-happens.aspx
- CNBC (Jan 2019), Sears chairman prevails in bankruptcy auction with $5.2 billion bid (425 stores, up to 45,000 jobs): https://www.cnbc.com/2019/01/16/sears-chairman-reportedly-prevails-in-bankruptcy-auction-for-retailer-with-5point2-billion-bid.html
- CoStar (July 2025), Once-giant Sears could soon be down to just five locations (eight stores left): https://www.costar.com/article/1406528706/once-giant-sears-could-soon-be-down-to-just-five-locations

Narrated with an AI voice. Researched and fact-checked by the Rise & Ruin team.

item.title: Toys R Us Was Bought With $5 Billion of Its Own Debt
item.itunes:title: Toys R Us Was Bought With $5 Billion of Its Own Debt
item.description:
In 2005, three investment firms bought Toys R Us for $6.6 billion. More than $5 billion of it was borrowed, and the toy store itself had to pay it back. Twelve years later, Toys R Us was bankrupt. Six months after that, all 735 of its American stores were closing.

This is the story of the toy store every child knew: the backwards R, the ten-year Amazon deal that went to court, the leveraged buyout, and the brand that refused to die.

Watch this Empire File with photos and documents on YouTube: https://youtu.be/PjyxjpOVxbk
Subscribe on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@riseundruin

Sources
- CNBC (Mar 2018), Toys R Us founder Charles Lazarus dies at 94 (1948 founding, 1957 first store, backwards R): https://www.cnbc.com/2018/03/22/toys-r-us-founder-charles-lazarus-dies-at-94-as-toy-empire-liquidates.html
- NPR (1999), Toys Were Us (losing ground to Walmart): https://www.npr.org/1999/11/28/1067149/toys-were-us
- Out-Law / Pinsent Masons (2006), Toysrus.com wins Amazon.com exclusivity suit: https://www.pinsentmasons.com/out-law/news/toysruscom-wins-amazoncom-exclusivity-suit
- TechCrunch (June 2009), Amazon pays $51 million to end battle with Toys R Us: https://techcrunch.com/?p=73108
- Forbes (Sept 2017), The big investment firms that lost $1.3 billion in the Toys R Us bankruptcy ($6.6B buyout, $5.3B+ debt, ~$400M a year, CEO filing quote): https://www.forbes.com/sites/nathanvardi/2017/09/19/the-big-investment-firms-that-lost-1-3-billion-on-the-toys-r-us-bankruptcy/
- CBS News (Mar 2018), Toys R Us shutting U.S. stores, liquidating inventory (735 stores, 33,000 jobs, $5B+ debt): https://www.cbsnews.com/news/toys-r-us-shutting-u-s-stores-liquidating-inventory/
- NPR (July 2022), Toys R Us is making another comeback, this time in Macy's stores: https://www.npr.org/2022/07/19/1112275498/toys-r-us-macys-stores
- Retail Brew (Nov 2025), Toys R Us is making a comeback (WHP Global, new stores): https://www.retailbrew.com/stories/2025/11/12/toys-r-us-is-making-a-comeback-and-toymakers-are-rejoicing

item.description:
In February 2008, Microsoft offered $44.6 billion for Yahoo. Yahoo said no. Eight years later, it agreed to sell its core internet business to Verizon for less than $5 billion.

This is the story of the company that was once the front door to the internet: how it put Google's name next to its own search box, offered $1 billion for Facebook and was turned down, rejected Microsoft, and then lost data from all three billion of its accounts.

item.title: Facebook Didn't Kill MySpace. MySpace Did
item.itunes:title: Facebook Didn't Kill MySpace. MySpace Did
item.description:
In July 2006, for one week, MySpace was the most visited website in America by one research firm's count, ahead of Google and Yahoo. News Corp had bought it a year earlier for $580 million. In 2011, it sold MySpace for about $35 million.

The usual story is that Facebook killed it. But MySpace was already hurting itself: a $900 million ad deal with traffic targets, twice as many ads, a product its own co-founder says lacked focus, and a rival that let others build on its platform. This is the rise and ruin of the social network that taught a generation how to live online.

item.title: Tata Tried to Sell to Ford. 9 Years Later, It Bought Jaguar
item.itunes:title: Tata Tried to Sell to Ford. 9 Years Later, It Bought Jaguar
item.description:
In 1999, Tata flew to Detroit to sell its struggling car business to Ford, and according to a Tata executive who was there, the meeting was humiliating. Nine years later, Ford was the one selling, and Tata bought Jaguar and Land Rover for $2.3 billion. Then the financial crisis hit.

This is the story of how an Indian company, famous for trucks and the world's cheapest car, turned two struggling British brands into a business earning billions, and why the story still isn't over.

item.title: WeWork: The $47 Billion Company That Rented Desks
item.itunes:title: WeWork: The $47 Billion Company That Rented Desks
item.description:
In 2019, WeWork was valued at $47 billion, the most valuable startup in America. It also owed about $47 billion in future rent. Six weeks after it filed to go public, its founder was gone and the IPO was dead.

This is the story of how a company that rented office desks convinced the world it was a tech giant, what investors found when they finally read the fine print, and why only one of those two 47s survived.

item.title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera. So Why Did It Go Bankrupt?
item.itunes:title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera. So Why Did It Go Bankrupt?
item.description:
